Herbs and their planetary rulers, the turning Wheel of the Year, the tools of the altar, and the words of power — gathered from the leechbooks, grimoires, and living practice of European witchcraft, and set down here leaf by leaf.

The Relic Itself

Hold the Book in Your Hand

Before the leaves, the object. A hand-bound grimoire modelled as it was actually made — boarded leather covers over a sewn page block, a rounded spine with raised bands, brass at the corners and clasps at the fore-edge, and the pentagram struck in relief on the front board, not printed on it. Drag it and turn it over. Open it. Turn its leaves. It is built to be handled.

Anatomy of this rendering

CoversTwo boards under tooled leather — procedural grain, mottling, and wear — with a gilt double-rule frame and the title set on the front board, as a binder finishes a book by hand.
The sealThe pentagram is raised relief geometry — five strokes and a double ring standing proud of the leather — not a picture printed on the cover. It catches the light as you turn the book, the way blind tooling does.
SpineRounded, with five raised bands where the sewing cords sit beneath the leather — the anatomy of a hand-sewn binding, visible when you turn the book to its spine.
Page blockIndividual leaf edges line the fore-edge; the leaves themselves are printed — a title leaf, the Wheel, and a herbal leaf — and they turn, one at a time, on the spine hinge.
BrassCorner pieces and two fore-edge clasps, modelled as metal with real reflections — the furniture that kept a working grimoire shut and safe.
RibbonA red silk marker falls from the spine foot past the fore-edge, as bound in.

Leaf the First

The Moon Tonight

Witches have always worked by her. Workings for growth are begun as she waxes; workings of banishing and ending as she wanes; and the full moon — the esbat — is the high tide of power. Her face below is drawn for this very night, computed from the true lunar cycle.

Leaf the Second

The Wheel of the Year

Eight festivals turn the year: four fixed fire festivals inherited from the Celtic calendar — Samhain, Imbolc, Beltane, Lughnasadh — and the solstices and equinoxes between them. Gerald Gardner and Ross Nichols joined the two sets into a single wheel in the 1950s; it has turned in covens ever since. Touch a spoke of the wheel.

❧

Leaf the Third

Materia Magica — The Herbal

Every plant in the witch's garden was known three ways: by its medicine, by its planet, and by its power. The correspondences below follow the tradition recorded in the old herbals and in modern practice — Culpeper's planetary rulerships, the Anglo-Saxon Nine Herbs Charm, and the lore of the flying ointments.

Read with care. Several plants in this herbal — belladonna, mandrake, foxglove among them — are deadly poisons. They are recorded here as they were recorded in the old books: as history and lore. Nothing in this leaf is an instruction to gather, prepare, or consume them.
♰

Leaf the Fourth

The Tools of the Altar

The working tools descend from the ceremonial grimoires — above all the Key of Solomon — by way of the Golden Dawn into Gardner's craft. Each belongs to an element, and each does one work: to direct, to invoke, to contain, to consecrate.

✦

Leaf the Fifth

Casting the Circle

Before any working, the circle is cast: a sphere of consecrated space, “a temple between the worlds,” raised the same way in coven after coven. Walk the rite step by step, as it is done.

✒

Leaf the Sixth

Words of Power & Candle Fire

The oldest spells in this book are a thousand years old and were written to be sung. Beside them, the candle colours of modern practice — light one, and read its meaning.

The Nine Herbs Charm

Lacnunga · Anglo-Saxon leechbook · 10th–11th century

“Gemyne ðu, mucgwyrt, hwæt þu ameldodest,
hwæt þu renadest æt Regenmelde.”
“Remember, Mugwort, what you made known, what you set out at Regenmeld.”

A healing song against poison and the “flying venom,” naming nine sacred plants — mugwort, plantain, lamb's cress, nettle, chamomile, crab apple, chervil, fennel — and the god Woden, who struck a serpent into nine pieces with nine glory-twigs. It is among the oldest surviving spells in English.

The Charge of the Goddess

Doreen Valiente, after Leland's Aradia · 1899 / 1950s

“Listen to the words of the Great Mother… I am the beauty of the green earth, and the white Moon among the stars, and the mystery of the waters.”

Charles Godfrey Leland claimed his Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches (1899) came from a Tuscan witch named Maddalena; historians still argue over how much he invented. Doreen Valiente reworked its charge into the text read in Wiccan circles today.

Leaf the Seventh

The Lineage of the Books

No grimoire stands alone. Each of these books copied, answered, or reinvented the ones before it — from an Anglo-Saxon sickroom to a Tuscan hillside to a cottage in the New Forest.

The Witch's Grimoire · an exhibit of the Divine Archives Herbal entries record historical lore, not instruction. Poisonous plants are marked as they deserve.
